doc.title: Butch Miles interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Opportunities for young players and sticking with it
summary: He discusses where young lions can play, George Wein's scouting, European work, and Buddy Rich's remark that the cream rises.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: Real quick. Are there any other venues on the way up for the young lions? Places for them to play, things for them to do, that authenticates the music and makes the music one with the culture. And if so, if not, what can be instituted?

Well that is a good one. There are different ways of getting your education, your musical education from the way I did starting out playing just in dance groups and dance bands and after-hour joints where you play a club that you couldn’t buy liquor by the drink it was illegal and you’d have to go and then everybody would fall by at midnight, 1:00 in the morning, 2:00 and jam sessions. But there’s a lot of different opportunities out now for a lot of the like you say “young lions.” Some of these jazz parties. Some of the jazz promoters. You hear some of these people but say this guy is really great but nobody knows who he is, I want to have him, or her for my party, bring them out. Other people get a chance to hear them. Some of the promoters like George Wein and others. George is still involved naturally with the JVC jazz festival in New York and he does some scouting around the country and hears a lot of people, loves to hire some of these guys like Nicholas Payton, fantastic young trumpet player out of New Orleans, you know or Wallace Roney or some of these other people, and bring them out and give them exposure. There’s different places to play, especially in the European market. We do a lot of traveling overseas. I was over in Europe last year, I think four times, four or five times I can’t recall. This year I’ll be in Europe two, maybe three times, and in Japan also. So there is some hope out there. They still have a lot of clubs. A lot of the nightclubs and entertainment areas around the United States have just gotten too expensive, people can’t afford it, the overhead is very high where these people are going to play. But Buddy Rich said it one time. Years ago someone asked him, said, “Buddy, we’ve got so many of these wonderful players coming out of the colleges and universities, where are they going to play? The clubs are all drying up and nothing’s happening. What are they going to do?” And Buddy said, “the cream always rises to the top.” I’ve run into a lot of people who’ve said, “yeah, I used to love to play music” or, “I play jazz, but that was 25 or 30 years ago

and then I graduated from college and I got married and I got the job and boy I sure am sorry I stopped.” I say, “I’m sorry you stopped, too, but don’t bitch to me about your stopping.” “I got out of college, I got a job, I got a family, so that’s why I had to quit playing.” “Oh, no, you don’t have to quit playing.” You see a whole lot of people out there who didn’t quit playing either. So you just — and it is tough, it is tough. You have to stick in this business, ‘cause it will kill you, it will just waste you away and then turn around and make your life so marvelous you can’t believe you ever thought of a rainy day as everything is sunshine and beautiful blue skies. And then maybe the next day you’re back with clouds and thunderstorms. I’m just using a weather analogy.
Well it does have its highs and lows.
